query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the uncharacterized high‐entropy alloy, the random, multi‐element arrangement creates locally varied lattice distortions that stabilize a uniform electronic density of states and enhance electron–phonon coupling. This drives the emergence of conventional (s‐wave) superconductivity at low temperatures. Reducing the configurational entropy (by omitting one principal element) will disrupt these favorable local environments and depress or suppress superconductivity.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy with a homogeneous body‐centered cubic (bcc) phase formed from five nearly equiatomic transition metals (e.g., similar in spirit to (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33) whose superconducting behavior is uncharacterized.
generation.intervention: Prepare two samples: one with the full high‐entropy composition and a controlled variant with reduced configurational entropy (e.g., by removing one of the principal elemental constituents while preserving overall phase and structure).
generation.conditions: Low-temperature regime (e.g., 2 K to 20 K) at ambient pressure, ensuring that structural phase remains unchanged.
generation.structural_mediator: The inherently stable bcc lattice and local lattice distortions induced by random elemental distribution.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy leads to a robust, disordered yet chemically homogeneous state that produces uniformly enhanced electron–phonon coupling. This promotes isotropic (s‐wave) Cooper pairing despite significant compositional randomness. In contrast, reducing entropy weakens these local fluctuations and disrupts the favorable interaction, lowering Tc or yielding an incomplete superconducting state.
generation.predicted_outcome: The full, high-entropy alloy will exhibit a sharp superconducting transition (zero electrical resistance and measurable diamagnetic response) at a specific Tc in the low-temperature regime. In contrast, the reduced-entropy variant will show a lower Tc, a broadened or incomplete transition, or possibly no superconducting phase under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The superconducting properties of the high-entropy alloy in its as-prepared, full compositional state (with maximum configurational entropy) serve as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should hold only when the alloy maintains a single, stable bcc phase (i.e., within specific temperature and pressure ranges where no structural transformation occurs). The hypothesis may not apply if the system is altered by high pressure, different crystallographic phases, or extreme compositional deviations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Tc value and the quantitative extent to which electron–phonon coupling is enhanced by high configurational entropy remain to be determined. The interplay with possible changes in carrier concentration and microscopic pairing interactions also introduces uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one retaining the full high-entropy alloy composition and the other a modified variant with one principal element removed (thereby reducing the configurational entropy) while maintaining the bcc structure. Perform low-temperature electrical resistivity measurements and magnetic susceptibility analyses on both samples to determine the superconducting transition characteristics.
measurements: Temperature-dependent four-probe resistivity (to detect zero resistance below Tc)
Heat capacity measurements (to capture superconducting anomaly)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of one element (i.e., reduction in configurational entropy) does not lead to a significant change (such as a lower Tc, a broadened transition, or suppressed superconductivity) compared to the full high-entropy sample, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy (and its induced local lattice distortions enhancing electron–phonon coupling) governs the emergence of superconductivity will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. Such a superconductor with a highly robust zero-resistance state, existing continuously from 1 atm to geological pressures, is extremely unusual and is in fact unique

A sharp drop to a zero-resistance superconducting state is observed at ∼7.7 K (we define TC as the temperature where the resistance changes from a finite value to zero), consistent with the results reported in ref. . Applying a magnetic field on the sample shows that its superconducting transition temperature (TC) systematically shifts to lower temperature (Fig. 1A, Inset), as expected. Temperature-dependent constant-current magnetic susceptibility characterization was also performed for the ambient-pressure sample. As shown in Fig. 1B, a strong diamagnetic response is observed starting at 7.6 K, indicative of a bulk superconducting nature. High-pressure resistance measurements were performed for four samples that were cut from the material used as the standard for the superconductivity at ambient pressure. The electrical resistance measurements for these samples were performed between 4 and 300 K. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. We have experimentally studied the superconducting state of the HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x In thin film form with x=0.35 and x=0.71 by measuring Hc1(T) and Hc2(T). Our analysis of λ(T) is in quantitative agreement with the BCS theory of an isotropic single band s-wave superconductor in the weak coupling limit. The analysis of ξ(T) reveals a comparable amount of disorder at both compositions, lx=0.35≈lx=0.71. Therefore, we can exclude that the observed variations in Tc originate from a disorder-driven mechanism. Further theoretical and experimental studies will be needed to characterize the low-energy electronic structure at various alloy compositions and its influence on Tc. Looking ahead, results of such efforts may inform pathways for realizing HEAs with enhanced superconducting Tc. Employing penetration-depth measurements to other superconducting HEAs, such as those crystallizing on the CsCl-type lattice, it will be interesting to test whether weak coupling s-wave superconductivity is a common occurrence in these material systems.
